title: Bea and Sol's Poetic Queue
markdown:
By a river that flowed like a gentle sigh lived a very busy beaver named Bea. Her fur was the colour of pebbles after a soft rain. Her paws were as busy as a little clock. Every day her life’s great work was to tend her magnificent dam: a sturdy wall of finest twigs and stickiest mud that pooled the river into a calm pond, a smooth grey mirror for the sky. Dragonflies practised being jewels. The mud smelled honest.

On that pond lived Sol the swan, pure white, feathers as soft as freshly fallen snow. Her neck curved like a question mark pondering the breeze. When she glided, it looked less like swimming than dancing on water. Sometimes she and Bea did not speak. The pond did the speaking for them.

Bea patched a loose twig here, patted mud there. Sol stretched, preened, drifted. A perfectly balanced, wonderfully quiet life.

Then a rumbling began. A great noisy ferry terminal, clanging metal and puffing steam, sprouted by the riverbank near Bea’s pond. With the terminal came people. Lots and lots of people.

Every day the sensible peaceful routine began to wobble. Bea’s dam felt strange new ripples. Water levels went up and down like a nervous heartbeat when a large ferry passed too close. Sol, who loved her smooth elegant glides, had to swerve and dip to avoid the messy wake. Not at all elegant.

At the terminal, ticket clerk Ms. Flint wore a smart blue uniform, spectacles perched on the tip of her nose. Her mission was to make sure everyone formed a sensible line. “One at a time, please. No dawdling.”

But these passengers were peculiar. They were not only waiting for a ride. They stood by the water’s edge, gazing as if dreaming. They scribbled in little notebooks, brows furrowed, murmuring. Ms. Flint found this most vexing.

“And what, pray tell, are you doing?” she asked a gentleman staring at a duck as if it held the secrets of the universe.

“I am capturing the very essence of quackery,” he replied, as if discussing the weather. “Such profound depths in its simple quack.”

Another passenger sighed a long dramatic sigh. “The river’s song is so profound today.”

Ms. Flint puffed air that misted her spectacles and tapped her ticket machine. “The only song the river is singing is queue-jumping if you’re not careful.”

Bea, patching her dam, heard the distant chatter and Ms. Flint’s sharp pronouncements. A ferry hooted. The pond answered with a ripple that had opinions. Sol, paddling near the bank, watched faces soften when they looked at the water: a thoughtfulness, a quiet wonder, as if the river had lent them a spare heart for the afternoon.

Then came a particularly blustery Tuesday. Wind whipped. A large group arrived all at once, overflowing sketchpads, whispering about metaphors and similes, and one person who appeared to be interviewing a bollard. The queue stretched past the ice-cream stand and began to curl around the little lighthouse. Ms. Flint was well and truly at her wit’s end. These poets, as she had grudgingly begun to call them, were not forming a sensible line. They gathered in knots, pointing at clouds and the way water lapped the piers, as if piers had been invented for pointing.

“Right, that’s it. No more. This is utter chaos.” She wrung her hands, spectacles fogging. “My queue is not sensible. It’s a poem.”

Bea felt a strange tug. Paws twitched. Tail flicked. She waddled out from behind her dam, sturdy paws in damp mud, and looked at the jumble. An idea took root: a dam-building idea, but for people.

Sol, seeing Bea’s focused gaze, felt it too. Her usual gentle notes tightened, sharper, more insistent: a call to action.

“Bea,” called Ms. Flint, breathless. “Can you possibly do something? My queue is unravelling.”

Bea pointed her wet nose toward a more open space. “The water needs a new channel. A tidier one. A more organised flow.” She began nudging stray logs washed ashore, showing how they could be arranged: not a wall to keep people out, but a path to keep them from bumping. Stick here. Stick there. The same patience she used on leaks.

Sol’s calls wove a gentle magic. People stopped staring at clouds and looked where those beautiful clear notes led. A child copied a swan-neck with an arm and was gently discouraged by a parent, then by Sol, who was politer. Damp wood of the pier felt steady. Papers, once scattered, held neat purposeful lines. They began to move, almost as if pulled by an invisible melodious string, toward Bea’s log arrangement. It started to resemble a very neat, very short queue, which is a rare and precious kind of miracle.

Slowly, then more surely, they gathered in order, inspired by Bea’s structure and Sol’s melody. One man, inspired by dam-building, sketched blueprints for a fortress of verse. Another, captivated by Sol’s soaring calls, started a poem about the melody of the ferry’s horn. A third discovered that standing behind someone was not, after all, a metaphor, but a practical kindness. They were becoming poets of the pier, which still required tickets, a fact Ms. Flint appreciated with her whole uniform.

Ms. Flint blinked behind fogged spectacles. Her queue was now perfectly sensible. Water, guided by Bea’s logs, flowed gently around the edges. The passengers were writing, yes, but also organised, content. She adjusted her spectacles, a small surprised smile playing.

“Well. That’s certainly a sensible kind of chaos.”

Bea discovered a knack for directing orderly lines with dam-building logic. Sol found her calls could inspire not only swans but humans to find their own rhythm. From that day the ferry terminal hummed with a gentler, more creative energy. Ferries still chugged. Ice cream still dripped, poetically. By the riverbank you could often find a beaver arranging ticket holders in a perfect line, and a swan singing the opening of a new ballad. Bea and Sol wondered what else might flow, if given a tidy channel and a clear note.
characters: Bea (a pebble-furred beaver), Sol (an elegant pond swan), Ms. Flint (a queue-keeping ticket clerk)
